title: Organic Compounds containing Nitrogen
tagline: Amine basicity, Hofmann and Gabriel synthesis, Hinsberg and carbylamine tests, and diazonium salts as the gateway to substituted aromatic rings.

overview.intro: Amines are organic derivatives of ammonia in which one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by alkyl or aryl groups, and they are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary according to how many of the three hydrogens have been replaced. The nitrogen atom in an amine is sp3 hybridised and pyramidal, with a lone pair occupying the fourth position, and that lone pair is what makes amines basic and nucleophilic. The whole unit turns on two properties of that lone pair: its availability to a proton, which determines basicity, and its availability to an electrophile such as an alkyl halide or an acid chloride, which determines the reactions. Basicity is subtle because it depends on the medium: in water the order for the methylamines is secondary, then primary, then tertiary, then ammonia, while in the gas phase the order is tertiary, then secondary, then primary, then ammonia, and aniline is far weaker than ammonia because its lone pair is delocalised into the ring. The unit covers the preparation of amines by the Gabriel phthalimide synthesis, Hofmann bromamide degradation, reduction of nitriles and nitro compounds, and substitution of alkyl halides; the reactions of amines with acids, alkyl halides, acid chlorides and nitrous acid; the Hinsberg and carbylamine tests that distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary amines; the chemistry of cyanides and isocyanides; and the preparation and synthetic importance of diazonium salts through the Sandmeyer, Gattermann and Balz-Schiemann reactions and azo coupling.

learningOutcomes: Classify amines as primary, secondary or tertiary and as aliphatic or aromatic, and name them by the IUPAC and common systems.
Describe the structure of the amino group and explain why amines are basic and nucleophilic.
Describe the preparation of amines by the Gabriel phthalimide synthesis, Hofmann bromamide degradation, reduction of nitriles and nitro compounds, and reaction of ammonia with alkyl halides.
Compare the basic strength of primary, secondary and tertiary amines with ammonia and aniline, and explain the effect of substituents on the basicity of aniline.
Describe the reactions of amines with acids, alkyl halides, acid chlorides and nitrous acid, and use the Hinsberg and carbylamine tests to identify primary, secondary and tertiary amines.
Distinguish cyanides from isocyanides and describe their methods of preparation.
Describe the preparation of diazonium salts and their reactions through Sandmeyer, Gattermann and Balz-Schiemann, and explain their importance in synthesis.

learn.title: Classification, structure and nomenclature of amines

blocks.text: Amines are classified by the number of hydrogens of ammonia that have been replaced by organic groups. A primary amine has one group and the formula RNH2, a secondary amine has two groups and the formula R2NH, and a tertiary amine has three groups and the formula R3N. A quaternary ammonium salt has four groups and carries a positive charge on nitrogen. Amines are also classified by the nature of the group: aliphatic amines have alkyl groups, aromatic amines have the nitrogen attached directly to a benzene ring, and mixed amines have both. Aniline, C6H5NH2, is the parent aromatic amine, and its derivatives are named as substituted anilines, while the aliphatic amines are named as alkylamines in the common system and as alkanamines in the IUPAC system.

The nitrogen atom of an amine is sp3 hybridised and the molecule is pyramidal, with bond angles close to the tetrahedral angle and the lone pair occupying the fourth position. Because the lone pair is not used in bonding, it is available to accept a proton, which makes amines basic, and to attack an electrophilic carbon, which makes them nucleophilic. The pyramidal geometry is not rigid: the nitrogen passes through a planar transition state in which the lone pair is in a p orbital, and the three groups invert from one side to the other. This inversion is very fast for simple amines, so an amine with three different groups cannot be resolved into stable enantiomers, though bulky groups slow the inversion enough for resolution in some cases.

items.meaning: An amine of the form RNH2, in which nitrogen is bonded to one carbon group and two hydrogens.
An amine of the form R2NH, in which nitrogen is bonded to two carbon groups and one hydrogen.
An amine of the form R3N, in which nitrogen is bonded to three carbon groups and carries no hydrogen.
A salt of the form R4N+X-, in which all four positions around nitrogen are occupied by carbon groups.
An amine in which the nitrogen is attached directly to an aromatic ring, so the lone pair can be delocalised into that ring.

items: Primary and secondary amines form intermolecular hydrogen bonds through the N-H group, so they boil higher than tertiary amines and much higher than alkanes of similar mass.
Tertiary amines have no N-H bond, so they cannot donate a hydrogen bond and boil lower than their primary and secondary isomers.
Amines boil lower than alcohols of similar mass, because nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen and its hydrogen bonds are weaker.
Lower amines are soluble in water because the nitrogen lone pair accepts hydrogen bonds from water molecules.
Lower aliphatic amines have a fishy smell, and the smell becomes less pronounced as the chain length increases.

blocks.text: The simplest preparation, the reaction of ammonia with an alkyl halide, is also the least satisfactory, because the primary amine first formed is a better nucleophile than ammonia and reacts again, giving a mixture of primary, secondary and tertiary amines and finally a quaternary ammonium salt. A large excess of ammonia improves the yield of the primary amine but does not eliminate the mixture. Reduction of a nitrile with lithium aluminium hydride or with hydrogen over nickel gives a primary amine with the same number of carbons as the nitrile, and reduction of a nitro compound with hydrogen over nickel, or with tin and hydrochloric acid, gives a primary aromatic amine, which is how aniline is made from nitrobenzene.

Two named methods give a pure primary amine. Hofmann bromamide degradation treats an amide with bromine and potassium hydroxide, and the product is a primary amine with one carbon fewer than the amide, because the carbonyl carbon is lost as carbonate. The reaction is useful for stepping down a homologous series and gives a pure primary amine without contamination by secondary or tertiary products. The Gabriel phthalimide synthesis starts from phthalimide, which is converted into potassium phthalimide by potassium hydroxide. The imide nitrogen is now a good nucleophile, so it displaces the halide from a primary alkyl halide to give an N-alkylphthalimide, and hydrolysis with acid or alkali then releases the primary amine and regenerates phthalic acid. The Gabriel synthesis works only for aliphatic amines, because aryl halides are not reactive enough towards nucleophilic substitution.

items: From ammonia and an alkyl halide, giving a mixture of primary, secondary and tertiary amines and a quaternary salt.
From an alkyl halide with potassium cyanide followed by reduction of the nitrile, which lengthens the chain by one carbon.
From an amide by Hofmann bromamide degradation: RCONH2 + Br2 + 4 KOH gives RNH2 + K2CO3 + 2 KBr + 2 H2O.
From phthalimide by the Gabriel synthesis: potassium phthalimide with R-X gives an N-alkylphthalimide, which is hydrolysed to RNH2.
From a nitro compound by reduction: C6H5NO2 with hydrogen over nickel, or with tin and hydrochloric acid, gives C6H5NH2.
From an alcohol and ammonia at high temperature over a catalyst, which is the industrial route to lower alkylamines.

items.text: How would you prepare a pure sample of butan-1-amine from butanamide?
items.note: Butanamide treated with bromine and potassium hydroxide undergoes Hofmann bromamide degradation, losing the carbonyl carbon as carbonate and giving propan-1-amine, not butan-1-amine. To obtain butan-1-amine from butanamide a different route is needed: dehydrate the amide to butanenitrile with phosphorus pentoxide and then reduce the nitrile, which keeps the four-carbon chain.

items.text: Why cannot the Gabriel synthesis be used to prepare aniline?
items.note: The Gabriel synthesis requires nucleophilic substitution of the halide by the phthalimide nitrogen, and aryl halides are unreactive towards nucleophilic substitution because of the strength of the C-Cl bond and the instability of a phenyl cation. Aniline is therefore made by reducing nitrobenzene instead.

blocks.text: The basicity of an amine is the availability of its nitrogen lone pair for accepting a proton, and it is measured by the pKb of the conjugate acid: a smaller pKb means a stronger base. Three factors decide the availability of that lone pair. The first is the electron-releasing effect of alkyl groups, which increases the electron density on nitrogen and should increase basicity. The second is the solvation of the conjugate ammonium ion, which stabilises the ion and increases basicity, and it is more effective for ions with more N-H bonds. The third is steric hindrance, which makes it harder for a bulky proton to reach the nitrogen and for solvent molecules to solvate the ion.

In water the order for the methylamines is dimethylamine, then methylamine, then trimethylamine, then ammonia. Going from ammonia to methylamine the electron-releasing effect dominates and basicity rises; going from methylamine to dimethylamine it rises again; but going to trimethylamine the loss of solvation and the steric hindrance of three methyl groups outweigh the extra electron release, so the basicity falls below that of dimethylamine and even below that of methylamine. In the gas phase, where solvation plays no part, the order is simply trimethylamine, then dimethylamine, then methylamine, then ammonia, because only the electron-releasing effect operates.

Aniline is a far weaker base than ammonia. The nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance, so it is less available to a proton, and the conjugate acid formed by protonation loses that resonance stabilisation. The same delocalisation explains why aniline is much weaker than cyclohexylamine, in which the nitrogen is attached to an sp3 carbon and cannot donate its lone pair into a ring. Substituents on the ring modify this: an electron-releasing group such as methyl or methoxy increases the electron density on nitrogen and increases basicity, while an electron-withdrawing group such as nitro decreases it sharply, so 4-nitroaniline is a far weaker base than aniline and 4-methylaniline is a stronger one.

far weaker, because the lone pair is delocalised into the ring

items: In aqueous solution the basicity order for methylamines is secondary > primary > tertiary > ammonia.
In the gas phase the order is tertiary > secondary > primary > ammonia, because solvation is absent.
Aniline is much weaker than ammonia and than aliphatic amines, because resonance delocalises the nitrogen lone pair into the ring.
Electron-releasing substituents on the ring increase the basicity of aniline, and electron-withdrawing substituents decrease it.
The order of basicity of the three classes cannot be stated without specifying the medium and the groups involved.

items.text: Arrange ammonia, methylamine, dimethylamine, trimethylamine and aniline in order of increasing basicity in aqueous solution.
items.note: The order is aniline, then ammonia, then trimethylamine, then methylamine, then dimethylamine. Aniline is weakest because of resonance, and among the methylamines the balance of electron release against solvation and steric hindrance places dimethylamine at the top.

items.text: Why is cyclohexylamine a much stronger base than aniline?
items.note: In cyclohexylamine the nitrogen is attached to an sp3 carbon, so its lone pair cannot be delocalised into the ring and is fully available for protonation. In aniline the nitrogen is attached to an sp2 ring carbon and its lone pair is delocalised into the aromatic pi system, so it is much less available and the base is much weaker.

learn.title: Reactions of amines, the Hinsberg test, cyanides and isocyanides

blocks.text: Amines react as nucleophiles and as bases. With acids they form salts, which is how amines are separated from neutral compounds and how they are purified. With alkyl halides they undergo alkylation, and because the product is a stronger nucleophile than the starting amine the reaction tends to run on to the quaternary salt unless the alkyl halide is limited. With acid chlorides and anhydrides they undergo acylation, in which the nitrogen lone pair attacks the carbonyl carbon and an amide is formed; the amide is much less nucleophilic and less basic than the amine, so acylation stops after one step and is used to protect the amino group. Both alkylation and acylation are nucleophilic substitutions at the electrophilic carbon, and both are favoured by the availability of the nitrogen lone pair. In alkylation, the lone pair on nitrogen attacks the electrophilic carbon of an alkyl halide (nucleophilic substitution), giving an alkylated ammonium species which on deprotonation yields a higher amine. In acylation, the lone pair on nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon of an acid chloride or acid anhydride to form a tetrahedral intermediate that eliminates a leaving group (Cl− or carboxylate), giving an amide (e.g. aniline with ethanoyl chloride/acetic anhydride gives acetanilide).

The reaction with nitrous acid, generated in situ from sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid, is the basis of the identification of amines. A primary aliphatic amine reacts to give a diazonium salt that decomposes at once, releasing nitrogen and giving an alcohol along with a mixture of alkenes. A primary aromatic amine gives a diazonium salt that is stable at low temperature, which is the starting point for the whole diazonium chemistry of the next section. A secondary amine, aliphatic or aromatic, gives a yellow oily N-nitrosamine. A tertiary aliphatic amine gives no reaction apart from salt formation, while a tertiary aromatic amine undergoes nitration of the ring. The visible evolution of nitrogen therefore indicates a primary amine, and a yellow oil indicates a secondary amine.

The Hinsberg test uses benzenesulphonyl chloride to separate the three classes. A primary amine reacts to give an N-alkylbenzenesulphonamide that still has a hydrogen on nitrogen, and that hydrogen is acidic enough for the compound to dissolve in aqueous alkali as a sulphonamide salt. A secondary amine reacts to give an N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamide with no hydrogen on nitrogen, so it does not dissolve in alkali. A tertiary amine has no hydrogen on nitrogen and cannot react at all, so it remains as an insoluble amine or dissolves only as its own salt in the acid used. The carbylamine test is specific for primary amines: heating with chloroform and alcoholic potassium hydroxide gives an isocyanide, which has a very offensive smell.

blocks.caption: Table: Behaviour of amines in the Hinsberg test
columns: Solubility of the product in alkali
rows: soluble, because the N-H is acidic

items: Aniline with hydrochloric acid gives anilinium chloride, and with sulphuric acid gives the hydrogen sulphate, which shows its basic character.
Acetylation of aniline with acetic anhydride gives acetanilide, and benzoylation with benzoyl chloride gives benzanilide.
Aniline with bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline as a white precipitate, because the amino group activates the ring strongly.
Nitration and sulphonation of aniline give mainly the meta products in strong acid, because the anilinium ion formed there is meta-directing.
Cyanides: prepared from an alkyl halide with potassium cyanide, or by dehydrating an amide with phosphorus pentoxide.
Isocyanides: prepared from an alkyl halide with silver cyanide, or from a primary amine by the carbylamine reaction.
Cyanides have the group -C=N with the carbon attached to the alkyl group, while isocyanides have -N=C with the nitrogen attached to the alkyl group.
Cyanides are hydrolysed to carboxylic acids and reduced to primary amines, while isocyanides are hydrolysed to primary amines and formic acid and are reduced to secondary amines.

items.text: How would you distinguish aniline, N-methylaniline and N,N-dimethylaniline?
items.note: The carbylamine test is positive only for aniline, because only a primary amine gives the foul-smelling isocyanide. The Hinsberg test then separates the remaining two: N-methylaniline is secondary and gives a sulphonamide that is insoluble in alkali, while N,N-dimethylaniline is tertiary and gives no sulphonamide at all.

items.text: Why is acylation used to protect an amino group during the nitration of aniline?
items.note: In strong acid aniline is protonated to the anilinium ion, which is meta-directing, so direct nitration gives mainly meta nitroaniline and much oxidation. Acetylation converts the amine into acetanilide, whose amide group is less basic and less easily oxidised and which directs ortho and para, so nitration followed by hydrolysis gives para nitroaniline cleanly.

blocks.text: Tests and uses of aniline: as a primary aromatic amine, aniline gives a positive carbylamine test with chloroform and alcoholic KOH producing foul-smelling phenyl isocyanide, and with bromine water it gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline due to strong activation of the ring. On diazotisation followed by coupling with an alkaline phenol (e.g. β-naphthol) it forms an azo dye (a characteristic test/application of aromatic primary amines). Aniline is used in the manufacture of dyes, drugs, and polymers (e.g. in polyurethane and rubber-processing chemicals).

learn.title: Diazonium salts: preparation, reactions and synthetic importance

blocks.text: A diazonium salt has the group -N2+ attached to an aromatic ring, with a negative counter-ion such as chloride. Benzenediazonium chloride is prepared by diazotisation: aniline is dissolved in dilute hydrochloric acid and treated with sodium nitrite at 273 to 278 K, when nitrous acid generated in situ reacts with the amine to give the diazonium salt. The low temperature is essential, because the salt decomposes above about 283 K to give phenol and nitrogen, and it is used immediately after preparation rather than stored. Diazonium salts are relatively stable when the ring carries electron-withdrawing groups and much less stable when it carries electron-releasing groups.

The synthetic value of a diazonium salt is that the diazonium group can be replaced by an enormous range of other groups, which makes it a gateway from aniline to almost any substituted benzene. Replacement by chlorine or bromine uses copper(I) chloride or copper(I) bromide in the Sandmeyer reaction. Replacement by chlorine or bromine can also be done with copper powder in the presence of the corresponding hydrogen halide, which is the Gattermann reaction. Replacement by fluorine uses tetrafluoroboric acid to give the diazonium tetrafluoroborate, which is isolated and then heated to decompose it into the aryl fluoride; this is the Balz-Schiemann reaction. Replacement by iodine uses potassium iodide with warming, replacement by hydroxyl uses warm water or dilute acid, replacement by hydrogen uses hypophosphorous acid, and replacement by a nitro group uses sodium nitrite in the presence of copper.

The other great reaction of diazonium salts is coupling. In the presence of a phenol or an aromatic amine the diazonium ion acts as an electrophile and attacks the activated ring at the para position, giving an azo compound with the two rings joined by the -N=N- group. Coupling with phenol is carried out in mild alkali, where the phenoxide ion is the reactive species, and coupling with aniline is carried out in weakly acidic solution. The products are intensely coloured, usually orange or red, and they are the basis of azo dyes. Because the diazonium group can be replaced by so many different groups and can also be used to join two rings, diazonium chemistry is the standard route for preparing substituted benzenes that cannot be made by direct electrophilic substitution.

items: Sandmeyer reaction: C6H5N2Cl with copper(I) chloride gives chlorobenzene and nitrogen.
Sandmeyer bromination: C6H5N2Cl with copper(I) bromide gives bromobenzene.
Gattermann reaction: C6H5N2Cl with copper powder and hydrochloric acid gives chlorobenzene.
Balz-Schiemann reaction: C6H5N2Cl with tetrafluoroboric acid gives the diazonium tetrafluoroborate, which on heating gives fluorobenzene.
Replacement by iodine: C6H5N2Cl with potassium iodide gives iodobenzene.
Replacement by hydroxyl: warming with water gives phenol.
Replacement by hydrogen: hypophosphorous acid gives benzene.
Replacement by a nitro group: sodium nitrite with copper gives nitrobenzene.
Coupling with phenol in mild alkali gives p-hydroxyazobenzene, an orange dye.
Coupling with aniline in weak acid gives p-aminoazobenzene, a yellow dye.

items.text: How would you convert aniline into 4-bromophenol?
items.note: Aniline is diazotised with sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid at 273 to 278 K to give benzenediazonium chloride, and the salt is then treated with copper(I) bromide in the Sandmeyer reaction to give bromobenzene. Direct bromination would give a mixture, so the diazonium route is used to place the bromine cleanly. Converting the bromobenzene to 4-bromophenol would then require the Dow conditions, which shows why the order of steps matters in synthesis.

items.text: Why is the diazonium salt kept at 273 to 278 K and used at once?
items.note: Above about 283 K the diazonium group reacts with water to give phenol and nitrogen, and the salt can also decompose to give tarry material, so the yield falls rapidly. Keeping the solution ice-cold and using it immediately avoids both losses.

keyPoints: Amines are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary by the number of hydrogens of ammonia replaced by organic groups.

In water the methylamines are more basic than ammonia in the order dimethylamine > methylamine > trimethylamine > ammonia; in the gas phase the order is trimethylamine > dimethylamine > methylamine > ammonia.
Aniline is far weaker than ammonia because its lone pair is delocalised into the aromatic ring.
Electron-releasing substituents increase the basicity of aniline and electron-withdrawing substituents decrease it.
The Gabriel phthalimide synthesis and Hofmann bromamide degradation both give pure primary amines, the second with one carbon less.
The Hinsberg test with benzenesulphonyl chloride distinguishes primary, secondary and tertiary amines, and the carbylamine test is specific for primary amines.
Primary amines give nitrogen with nitrous acid, secondary amines give a yellow oily nitrosamine, and tertiary aliphatic amines do not react.
Diazonium salts are prepared from primary aromatic amines at 273 to 278 K and are the gateway to substituted benzenes through the Sandmeyer, Gattermann and Balz-Schiemann reactions.

questions.prompt: Which of the methylamines is the strongest base in aqueous solution?
questions.answer: Dimethylamine
questions.explanation: In water, basicity depends on the balance between the electron-releasing effect of methyl groups and the solvation of the conjugate ammonium ion. Dimethylamine has two methyl groups for electron release and two N-H bonds for solvation, so it is the strongest of the three, with trimethylamine the weakest because its ion is poorly solvated and its nitrogen is sterically crowded.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing trimethylamine by counting methyl groups alone, which gives the gas-phase order rather than the aqueous one.

questions.prompt: Aniline is a much weaker base than ammonia because:
options: aniline has a higher molecular mass than ammonia
the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring
the nitrogen atom is sp3 hybridised in aniline
questions.answer: the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring
questions.explanation: In aniline the nitrogen is attached to an sp2 ring carbon, so its lone pair participates in the aromatic pi system and is much less available for protonation. Protonation also destroys that resonance stabilisation, so the conjugate acid is relatively unstable and aniline is a weak base.
questions.commonMistake: Blaming insolubility, when aniline is basic in both water and acid and the real cause is electronic.

questions.prompt: The Hinsberg test uses:
questions.answer: benzenesulphonyl chloride
questions.explanation: Benzenesulphonyl chloride reacts with primary and secondary amines to give sulphonamides, and only the primary amine product retains an N-H that is acidic enough to dissolve in alkali. A tertiary amine does not react, so the test separates all three classes in one experiment.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing the Hinsberg reagent with the reagents of the carbylamine test.

questions.prompt: The Gabriel phthalimide synthesis is used to prepare:
questions.answer: primary aliphatic amines
questions.explanation: The phthalimide nitrogen is alkylated once by an alkyl halide and then released by hydrolysis, so the product carries only one alkyl group and is a pure primary amine. The method fails for aromatic amines because aryl halides do not undergo the required nucleophilic substitution.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming the method can make aniline, which must be prepared by reducing nitrobenzene.

questions.prompt: Hofmann bromamide degradation of propanamide gives:
questions.answer: ethylamine
questions.explanation: The reaction removes the carbonyl carbon of the amide as carbonate, so the amine produced has one carbon fewer than the amide. Propanamide, with three carbons, therefore gives ethylamine, with two.
questions.commonMistake: Expecting propylamine, which would keep the three-carbon chain.

questions.prompt: The carbylamine reaction is given by:
questions.answer: primary amines
questions.explanation: Heating a primary amine with chloroform and alcoholic potassium hydroxide gives an isocyanide, which has a very offensive smell. Secondary and tertiary amines have no N-H hydrogen to lose in the first step, so they do not give the reaction.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking that all amines give the carbylamine reaction.

questions.prompt: A secondary amine treated with nitrous acid gives:
questions.answer: a yellow oily N-nitrosamine
questions.explanation: A secondary amine has one hydrogen on nitrogen, which is replaced by the nitroso group to give an N-nitrosamine, an unstable yellow oil. A primary amine would give nitrogen and an alcohol, and a tertiary aliphatic amine would give only salt formation.
questions.commonMistake: Expecting a diazonium salt, which requires a primary aromatic amine.

questions.prompt: The Balz-Schiemann reaction converts benzenediazonium chloride into:
questions.answer: fluorobenzene
questions.explanation: The diazonium salt is treated with tetrafluoroboric acid to give the diazonium tetrafluoroborate, which is isolated and heated to decompose it into fluorobenzene and nitrogen. This is the standard route to aryl fluorides, which cannot be made by direct fluorination.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing it with the Sandmeyer reaction, which uses copper(I) halides for chlorine and bromine.

questions.prompt: Aniline treated with sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid at 273 to 278 K gives ______ chloride.
questions.answer: benzenediazonium
questions.explanation: The reaction is diazotisation: nitrous acid generated in situ converts the primary aromatic amine into the diazonium salt, which must be kept cold because it decomposes above about 283 K.
questions.commonMistake: Writing benzyl, which would imply the nitrogen is on a side chain rather than on the ring.

questions.prompt: Primary, secondary and tertiary amines are distinguished by the ______ test, using benzenesulphonyl chloride.
questions.answer: Hinsberg
questions.explanation: The Hinsberg test relies on the number of hydrogens on nitrogen: the primary amine gives a sulphonamide with an acidic N-H that dissolves in alkali, the secondary gives an insoluble sulphonamide, and the tertiary does not react.
questions.commonMistake: Writing carbylamine, which is specific to primary amines only.

questions.prompt: Hofmann bromamide degradation of an amide uses bromine together with ______.
questions.answer: potassium hydroxide
questions.explanation: The amide is treated with bromine in concentrated potassium hydroxide, which generates the bromamide intermediate that rearranges with loss of carbonate to give the primary amine.
questions.commonMistake: Writing hydrochloric acid, which would simply hydrolyse the amide to the carboxylic acid.

questions.prompt: Explain why aniline is a weaker base than ammonia.
questions.answer: In aniline the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance, so it is shared with the ring and is less available to accept a proton. Protonation would also destroy that resonance stabilisation, because the lone pair would then be committed to the N-H bond. Both effects make aniline much less willing to accept a proton than ammonia, whose lone pair is localised on nitrogen.
questions.explanation: The comparison is about the availability of the lone pair, and delocalisation into the ring is the feature that ammonia lacks entirely.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that aniline is less basic because it is aromatic, without explaining what the aromatic ring does to the lone pair.

questions.prompt: Why is the order of basicity of the methylamines in aqueous solution different from the order in the gas phase?
questions.answer: In the gas phase only the electron-releasing effect of the methyl groups matters, so basicity increases with the number of methyl groups and the order is trimethylamine, then dimethylamine, then methylamine. In aqueous solution the conjugate ammonium ion must be solvated, and solvation is strongest for ions with more N-H bonds, so the tertiary ammonium ion is poorly solvated. Steric hindrance also makes it harder for water to solvate the trimethylammonium ion, so in water the order becomes dimethylamine, then methylamine, then trimethylamine.
questions.explanation: The intrinsic basicity follows electron release, but the measured basicity in water also includes the energy of solvating the conjugate acid, and that term reverses the order at the top of the series.
questions.commonMistake: Giving one order without specifying the medium, when the medium decides the answer.

questions.prompt: Write the equations for the Sandmeyer and Gattermann reactions starting from benzenediazonium chloride.
questions.answer: In the Sandmeyer reaction, C6H5N2Cl with copper(I) chloride gives C6H5Cl + N2, and with copper(I) bromide it gives C6H5Br + N2. In the Gattermann reaction, C6H5N2Cl with copper powder and hydrochloric acid gives C6H5Cl + N2, and with hydrobromic acid it gives C6H5Br + N2. Both reactions replace the diazonium group by a halogen, the difference being the copper species used.
questions.explanation: Both are radical processes mediated by copper, so they achieve the same substitution and differ only in the reagent, which is why they are usually taught together.
questions.commonMistake: Omitting nitrogen as a product, which is the visible sign that the diazonium group has been lost.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a cyanide and an isocyanide with respect to structure and one reaction of each.
questions.answer: In a cyanide the alkyl group is attached to the carbon of the C=N group, giving R-CN, while in an isocyanide the alkyl group is attached to the nitrogen, giving R-NC. A cyanide is hydrolysed by dilute acid to a carboxylic acid and is reduced to a primary amine, whereas an isocyanide is hydrolysed to a primary amine and formic acid and is reduced to a secondary amine. Isocyanides also have a characteristic extremely unpleasant smell, which cyanides do not.
questions.explanation: The difference in which atom carries the alkyl group changes both the hydrolysis products and the reduction products, so the two families are genuinely distinct rather than alternative names.
questions.commonMistake: Treating cyanide and isocyanide as the same compound written two ways.

questions.prompt: Describe the Gabriel phthalimide synthesis and Hofmann bromamide degradation, and state one advantage of each.
questions.answer: In the Gabriel synthesis phthalimide is treated with potassium hydroxide to give potassium phthalimide, whose nitrogen is a good nucleophile. An alkyl halide displaces the halide and attaches its alkyl group to that nitrogen, giving an N-alkylphthalimide, and hydrolysis with acid or alkali releases the primary amine and regenerates phthalic acid. Its advantage is that it gives a pure primary amine without contamination by secondary or tertiary amines, though it works only for aliphatic amines. In Hofmann bromamide degradation an amide is treated with bromine and concentrated potassium hydroxide, and the product is a primary amine with one carbon fewer than the amide, the carbonyl carbon being lost as carbonate. Its advantage is that it provides a reliable one-carbon step down a homologous series while still giving a pure primary amine.
questions.explanation: Both methods are valued because they avoid the mixture of products that the ammonia and alkyl halide route produces, and each has a different structural consequence, one keeping the chain and one shortening it.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting that the Gabriel synthesis cannot be applied to aryl halides.

questions.prompt: Compare the basic strength of ammonia, methylamine, dimethylamine, trimethylamine and aniline in aqueous solution, and explain the position of aniline and the effect of substituents on it.
questions.answer: In water the order of increasing basicity is aniline, then ammonia, then trimethylamine, then methylamine, then dimethylamine. Methylamine and dimethylamine are stronger than ammonia because their methyl groups release electron density onto nitrogen, and dimethylamine is the strongest because it combines two methyl groups with two N-H bonds that allow good solvation of the conjugate acid. Trimethylamine is weaker than the other two methylamines because its conjugate acid has no N-H bond to solvate and the nitrogen is sterically crowded. Aniline is far weaker than ammonia because its lone pair is delocalised into the ring and protonation destroys that resonance. Substituents on the ring modify this: electron-releasing groups such as methyl or methoxy increase the basicity of aniline, while electron-withdrawing groups such as nitro decrease it sharply.
questions.explanation: The order is a balance of three effects, electron release, solvation and steric hindrance, and the aromatic amine adds a fourth, resonance delocalisation of the lone pair.
questions.commonMistake: Placing aniline above ammonia in the series, which would ignore the resonance delocalisation of its lone pair.

questions.prompt: Describe the preparation of benzenediazonium chloride and three of its reactions, and explain why diazonium salts are important in synthetic organic chemistry.
questions.answer: Aniline is dissolved in dilute hydrochloric acid and treated with sodium nitrite at 273 to 278 K, when nitrous acid generated in situ gives benzenediazonium chloride. With copper(I) chloride the salt undergoes the Sandmeyer reaction to give chlorobenzene, with potassium iodide it gives iodobenzene, and with warm water it gives phenol; other reagents replace the group by bromine, fluorine, hydrogen or a nitro group, and coupling with phenol gives an azo dye. The importance of diazonium salts is that they turn an amino group into a leaving group that can be replaced by almost any other substituent, so a single intermediate opens routes to substituted benzenes that cannot be made by direct electrophilic substitution, and it also allows two aromatic rings to be joined through an azo linkage.
questions.explanation: The synthetic value comes from the versatility of the diazonium group, which can be replaced by halogens, hydroxyl, hydrogen or nitro groups, or used to couple two rings.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the preparation without the temperature, which is the detail that decides whether the salt survives.

questions.prompt: Convert nitrobenzene into 4-bromoaniline, naming the reagents at each stage.
questions.answer: Nitrobenzene is reduced with hydrogen over a nickel catalyst, or with tin and hydrochloric acid followed by alkali, to give aniline. Aniline is then protected by acetylation with acetic anhydride to give acetanilide, which is less easily oxidised and directs ortho and para. Acetanilide is brominated with bromine in acetic acid to give 4-bromoacetanilide, and hydrolysis with dilute acid or alkali removes the acetyl group to give 4-bromoaniline. The protection step is necessary because direct bromination of aniline gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline.
questions.explanation: The acetyl group both moderates the reactivity of the ring and prevents oxidation of the amine, and its removal at the end restores the free amino group, so the sequence is reduction, protection, bromination and deprotection.
questions.commonMistake: Brominating aniline directly, which gives the tribromo product rather than the monobromo compound.

questions.prompt: A compound of molecular formula C7H9N is a monosubstituted benzene derivative. It gives no carbylamine reaction, gives a yellow oily product with nitrous acid, and forms a sulphonamide with benzenesulphonyl chloride that is insoluble in alkali. Identify the compound and explain each observation.
questions.answer: The compound is N-methylaniline. The absence of the carbylamine reaction shows that it is not a primary amine. The yellow oily product with nitrous acid is an N-nitrosamine, which is characteristic of a secondary amine. The formation of a sulphonamide that is insoluble in alkali confirms a secondary amine, because the sulphonamide has no N-H hydrogen to make it acidic. Of the C7H9N isomers, N-methylaniline is the only secondary amine, since toluidines are primary and N,N-dimethylaniline would give no sulphonamide at all.
questions.explanation: Each test narrows the class of amine, and the molecular formula then fixes which member of that class is present, so the three observations together identify a single structure.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing N,N-dimethylaniline, which is tertiary and would give no sulphonamide.

questions.prompt: Explain why a diazonium salt is prepared and used at 273 to 278 K, and what would happen if the solution were allowed to warm to room temperature before the Sandmeyer step.
questions.answer: The diazonium salt is thermally unstable: above about 283 K the diazonium group reacts with water to give phenol and nitrogen, and the salt can also decompose to tarry material. Preparing and using it in ice keeps the concentration of the intact salt high. If the solution warmed before the Sandmeyer step, much of the diazonium salt would be converted into phenol and nitrogen, so the yield of the Sandmeyer product would fall and the product would be contaminated with phenol and tar.
questions.explanation: The temperature control is not a matter of reaction rate but of the stability of the intermediate, so warming destroys the reagent rather than simply speeding up its use.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that the low temperature is needed to slow the reaction down, when it is needed to stop the salt decomposing.

questions.prompt: Arrange aniline, 4-methylaniline and 4-nitroaniline in order of increasing basicity and explain the order in terms of the availability of the nitrogen lone pair.
questions.answer: The order of increasing basicity is 4-nitroaniline, then aniline, then 4-methylaniline. In 4-nitroaniline the nitro group withdraws electron density strongly by both inductive and resonance effects, which reduces the electron density on nitrogen and makes the lone pair less available, so it is the weakest base. The methyl group of 4-methylaniline releases electron density, which increases the electron density on nitrogen and makes the lone pair more available, so it is the strongest of the three. Aniline lies between them because it has neither an electron-withdrawing nor an electron-releasing substituent.
questions.explanation: The para position is where the resonance effect of a substituent acts most directly on the ring carbon that bears the nitrogen, so para substituents have a large influence on basicity.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the order by treating the nitro group as electron releasing because it contains oxygen.
